Family: Amblycipitidae. Size: 5 cm. Temperature: 18–22°C. pH: 6.5–7.5. Distribution: Asia: China, Guangxi.

There are three species in the genus Xiurenbagrus: X. dorsalis, X. xiurenensis and X. gigas.

Asia: China, Guangxi. This species only occurs in one county and underground cave system in Guangxi Province, China. It is restricted to an area of occupancy and extent of occurrence of 4 km2, and only 1 threat-based location. All three species of the genus are distributed in the Pearl River basin.

Inhabits a very small underground stream with substrate of small rocks. The stream flows across the bottom of the well. A pump is connected to a 4 m depth well with plastic piping. The type specimen emerged through the water during pumping.

Xiurenbagrus dorsalis can be diagnosed from its congeners by the following combination of characters: 7 dorsal-fin branched rays (vs. 6 in X. xiurenensis and X. gigas); pelvic-fin origin opposite base of fourth branched dorsal-fin ray (pelvic-fin insertion posterior to dorsal-fin base in the other two species); serrations absent on the posterior edge of pectoral-fin spine (vs. strong serrations present); adipose fin confluent with caudal fin (vs. adipose fin posteriorly with a free flap and not confluent); maxillary barbel longer than head length and reaching posterior tip of pectoral-fin (vs. shorter than head length); eyes absent (vs. small eyes present). Dorsal soft rays (total): 8; anal soft rays: 12.

Though it is a blind catfish, it is placed in Xiurenbagrus because of the presence of two patches of vomerine teeth, a character not found in any other Amblycipitidae except the genus Xiurenbagrus.

Etymology: dorsalis refers to the unique position of the dorsal-fin origin (posterior to a vertical line at the tip of the pectoral fins) compared with its congeners.

IUCN Red List: the habitat is severely impacted by underground water use for agriculture by locals, and a continuing decline is inferred. The species is assessed as Critically Endangered and requires immediate protection (IUCN 2024).
